3.text:
Part 3
Question 19 to 26
You are going to read a recount of a person’s memory. Choose the correct answer A, B, C or
D and mark the correct answer on your answer sheet.
The first time I followed my grandfather to the night market in George Town, I was
barely ten. The air was thick with the smell of grilled satay, fried noodles, and incense drifting
from a nearby temple. My grandfather, whom everyone called Tok Ayah, walked slowly but
confidently, greeting almost every stall owner along the way. I did not understand then how he
seemed to belong everywhere.
“Stay close,” he said, glancing back at me with a gentle smile. “This place has many
line 6
stories, and you might get lost in them.” At one corner of the market stood a small, old stall
selling traditional Indian sweets. Bright orange jalebi curled like tiny suns, and squares of burfi
were stacked neatly on metal trays. Behind the stall was an elderly man with silver hair and
kind eyes.
“Arjun!” my grandfather called out warmly. The man looked up and broke into a wide
grin. “Ah, Hassan! You still come here every Friday night, I see.” I watched as they shook
hands, their laughter blending easily with the noise of the crowd. Tok Ayah bought a small box
of sweets and handed it to me. “These are special,” he said. “Not just because they’re delicious,
but because of who made them.”
I did not ask much then. To me, it was just another stop in a lively market. But every
week after that, we returned, and every time, the same exchange of smiles and stories took
place between the two men. Years passed, and life pulled me away. School, work, and
responsibilities slowly replaced those quiet Friday nights. Tok Ayah passed on when I was in
university, and with him, I thought, went those simple routines I had taken for granted.
One evening, many years later, I found myself back in George Town. The streets had
changed—cafés and murals had appeared but the night market was still there, glowing under
strings of yellow lights. On impulse, I walked through the familiar lanes, guided more by
memory than direction. And then I saw it—the same sweet stall. It looked smaller now, almost
fragile against the modern surroundings. The trays of sweets were still there, though fewer in
number. Behind the stall stood the same man, older, his movements slower but his eyes just as
kind.
I hesitated before stepping forward. “Uncle Arjun?” I asked softly. He looked up,
studying my face for a moment. Then his expression shifted. “You… Hassan’s grandson?” I
nodded, surprised that he remembered. He smiled, though there was a hint of sadness in it.
“You used to come here every week. You were always quiet, just watching everything.” I
laughed lightly. “I guess I still do that.”

He prepared a small box of sweets without asking. As he handed it to me, he said, “Your
grandfather was a good man. He believed people should never be strangers.” I looked around
line 34
at the bustling market—the mix of languages, the blend of cultures, the shared space that
somehow belonged to everyone. “I never really understood why he came here so often,” I
admitted.
Arjun leaned slightly on the counter. “During difficult times, many people kept to their
own communities. But your grandfather… he came here, talked to everyone, shared stories. He
said food and kindness were the easiest ways to bring people together.” For a moment, the
noise of the market seemed to fade. I could almost hear Tok Ayah’s voice again, telling me to
stay close.
“He told me once,” Arjun continued, “that traditions are not just about festivals or
clothes. They are about how we treat each other every day.” I swallowed, feeling a quiet weight
in my chest. “I wish I had asked him more.” Arjun nodded knowingly. “We always think there
will be more time.”
Before I left, I thanked him—not just for the sweets, but for the memories he had helped
preserve. As I walked away, I realised something had changed. The market no longer felt like
a place I was visiting. It felt like a place I belonged to. The next Friday, I returned.
This time, I did not just pass through. I stopped, I talked, and I listened—just as my
grandfather once did. And in that simple act, I understood what he had been trying to teach me
all along: that culture lives not only in traditions, but in the connections, we choose to keep
alive.

4.text:
Part 4
Question 27 to 32
You are going to read an article about how opposites attract each other. Six sentences have
been removed from the article. Choose from the sentences A to H the one which fits each gap
(27 to 32). There are two extra sentences which you do not need to use.
Some psychologists believe that we may be attracted to people who have qualities we
wish we had. For example, if you love music but do not play any instrument, you may feel
attracted to a musician. 27 Since people are complex, we can be attracted to different
kinds of people who are different from us in many ways. Let us look at three pairs of personality
qualities.
First, there are introverted and extroverted people. Introverted people often spend a lot
of time thinking about their own ideas and feelings. 28 Extroverted people enjoy going
out, meeting others, and spending time in social places. If opposites attract, introverted and
extroverted people may be interested in each other. 29 At the same time, extroverted
people may enjoy the peaceful and thoughtful world of introverted people.
Next, some people understand the world mainly by thinking, while others understand it
mainly by feeling. Thinkers are usually calm, logical, and fair when they make judgments.
Feelers are often warm, caring, and emotional. People who think a lot may also want to feel
more deeply. Because of this, they may be attracted to someone who is kind and emotional. In
the same way, a person with strong feelings may enjoy being with a relaxed and logical thinker.
Another pair is sensing and intuitive people. Sensing people use their five senses to
understand the world around them. They notice what is happening now and are usually realistic
and practical. 31 They use their imagination freely. Intuitive people may admire sensing
people because sensing people have practical skills that can help turn dreams into real plans.
Similarly, sensing people may admire intuitive people because they bring creative ideas and
new possibilities.
These three pairs, introvert and extrovert, thinker and feeler, sensor and intuitive, can
be found in every person. However, many psychologists believe that people usually use one
quality from each pair more often. 32 According to the idea that opposites attract, each
side needs the other.
Adapted from Interchange 5th Textbook

Question 33 to 40
The information below is about how money affects well-being. Read the text below and
answer all the questions that follow.
HOW MONEY AFFECTS WELL-BEING
A-MIZA, Model
I used to feel shy and awkward when talking to strangers because I was not confident about
my appearance. However, things began to change when I started receiving my salary.
Slowly, I started to attend social gatherings after transforming myself by buying new clothes
and accessories. This helped me to step out of my comfort zone and make new friends. As
time passed, my confidence grew stronger each day.
B-SYAFIQ, Businessman
Starting a business was a real challenge at first. I was afraid to ask my family for financial
support because I did not want to disappoint them. Then, my business began to grow and I
started earning a good income. Now, I feel proud of myself and happy because I am able to
support my family financially.
C – ANIS, Student
As a student, I can also see how money affects daily life. When students have enough pocket
money, they can join school activities, buy learning materials and enjoy social life with
friends. This makes them feel included and happy. On the other hand, students without
enough money may feel left out or stressed. Sometimes, they even avoid attending school
because they are afraid of being judged.
D-QIELA, University Student
From my point of view as a university student, money plays a significant role in shaping
happiness, especially in higher education. Many students struggle with tuition fees,
accommodation and daily expenses. When financial support is available, students can focus
better on their studies without constantly worrying about money. Therefore, while money is
not everything, it certainly helps reduce stress and creates a more balanced and enjoyable
life.
E – ZANA, School Counsellor
I often meet students who face emotional stress due to financial problems at home. Some of
them feel worried about their family situation, which affects their focus in school and their
happiness in daily life. When financial support is provided, these students often show
positive emotional changes. However, I also remind students that happiness should not
depend only on money.
F-ADIB, School Principal
I encounter many cases involving students who struggle with financial difficulties. To
address this issue, the school has launched a financial support fund and this support helps to
reduce their financial burden and encourages them to remain in school consistently. As a
result, this improves the students’ attendance and they become happier than before.
